n: David had resolved to guard his speech so he wouldn’t sin in front of the wicked, keeping his mouth muzzled like an animal with a bridle. The heading names Jeduthun, one of David’s temple musicians.

f.w: keep my mouth with a bridle

n: He stayed completely silent, saying nothing at all — not even good things. But keeping it all in only stirred up his pain.
His heart grew hot like a fire as he brooded, until finally the words burst out — in prayer to God rather than in complaints to people.

f.w: while I was musing the fire burned

n: His request: help me understand how short and fragile my life is. Recognizing our mortality helps us live wisely.

f.w: make me to know mine end

n: Life is only a few fingers wide in God’s sight. Even at our strongest, we are a passing breath.

f.g: The width of a hand — one of the smallest measures.
Hebrew hevel — a breath or vapor, the key word of Ecclesiastes.

n: People walk around like shadows, fussing over nothing. They pile up wealth without knowing who will end up with it.

f.w: knoweth not who shall gather them

n: The turning point: if life is so brief, what am I really hoping for? Only you, Lord.
He asks to be freed from all his sins and not to become a laughingstock for fools.
He fell silent because he recognized God’s hand in his trial — not to sulk, but in submission.
Still, he pleads: take your hand of discipline off me; I am worn out by it.
When God corrects sin, the things people treasure fade away like cloth eaten by a moth. Every human being is but a breath.

f.g: As a moth eats away a garment — quietly and completely.

n: A moving plea: don’t ignore my tears. David calls himself a guest and a traveler passing through God’s land, as his ancestors were.

f.g: A resident foreigner, a guest without permanent rights.

n: He asks for a little relief so he can smile again before he dies. The psalm ends raw and honest, without a tidy resolution.
